item.title: Council of State rejects reopening of FFS stop in Giornico
item.description: BELLINZONA - The Council of State rules out reopening a railway stop in Giornico.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The Council of State rejects reopening in Giornico - Line 120 serves Paese, Fraggio and Scuola Media - TILO connections transfer from the S10 at Biasca - No feasibility study will be initiated
## Key facts - Location → Giornico - Outcome → reopening not justified - Response → Council of State - Bus service → AutoPostale, line 120 - TILO connection → S10 at Biasca - Reactivated stops → Ambrì-Piotta, Lavorgo and Bodio - Recent request → Rodi-Fiesso station - Traffic → IR Locarno-Zurich/Basel
### The response on Giornico
BELLINZONA - The Council of State rules out reopening a railway stop in Giornico. The position is set out in the response to the interpellation submitted last December by Alessandro Corti, a Centre deputy, with Guerra and Tenconi as co-signatories. The parliamentary motion concerned rail accessibility and the historical-cultural enhancement of the Leventina village.
The Government justifies the refusal by citing the existing service offering and the assessment of railway operating costs. Giornico has the Giornico, Paese and Giornico, Fraggio stops; AutoPostale line 120 also runs scheduled services to Giornico, Scuola Media. The timetable presented by the Executive provides hourly services during off-peak hours and every half hour during the morning and evening peak periods.
The reference to line 120 is also precise in terms of locations: the response does not speak only of Giornico in general, but identifies Paese, Fraggio and Scuola Media. The rationale therefore considers both the stops served and the way they are connected to the TILO network.
This arrangement is complemented by connections described as being optimally linked to the TILO network, particularly with the S10 line at Biasca. The response therefore presents, within the same framework, the local stops, the varying frequency depending on the time of day and the interchange with the railway network. These are the elements used by the Council of State to argue that the settlement is already well served by public transport.
For the Government, the reopening proposal is not sustainable in light of operating requirements and costs. Consequently, the Council of State also declines to commission a feasibility or pre-feasibility study, as requested by the parliamentary motion.
The comparison with the parliamentary request is therefore twofold: the motion called for reopening to be examined and a preliminary analysis to be launched; the response considers the first scenario unjustified and declines the second. The two conclusions are attributed to the aspects explicitly indicated: operations and costs. The result communicated in Bellinzona is specific: for Giornico, the road-based service and connections with TILO are considered sufficient by the cantonal Government to make railway reopening unjustified. ## The precedent of the mountain line
### From 2016 to the return of the stops
The decision regarding Giornico comes within a broader reconstruction of the historic Gotthard line. The State Council begins with the opening of the base tunnel: inaugurated on June 1, 2016, it became accessible to passenger traffic in December of the same year.
| Moment | Facts recalled | |---|---| | June 1, 2016 | Inauguration of the base tunnel | | December 2016 | Access to passenger traffic | | After the opening | Hourly passenger service maintained on the mountain line | | Following year | Reactivation of the Bodio stop |
According to FFS plans, the opening of the new tunnel would have meant the cessation of service on the mountain route. The cantonal government's intervention nevertheless made it possible to maintain an hourly passenger service on the line. The response identifies this step as the starting point for the configuration described for Leventina after the opening of the tunnel.
Airolo and Faido were already existing stations. After the inauguration of the base tunnel, Ambrì-Piotta and Lavorgo were instead reactivated; Bodio followed the following year. The sequence identifies three reopenings, different in location but attributed by the Government to the same rationale: integration with the bus network. The same State Council characterizes them as an exception for a non-commissioned railway service.
The comparison with Giornico is viewed within this sequence. The three stops are not presented merely as additions to the line, but as reopenings decided primarily in relation to bus connections. For Giornico, by contrast, the response refers to the AutoPostale service and the TILO connections already available; the documented point is therefore the different outcome attributed to a new reopening compared with the three reactivations already carried out.
The institutional distinction indicated by the Government also concerns the trains that run on the line. Long-distance traffic includes Eurocity, Intercity and Interregio services: these services are planned by the Confederation, fall within the FFS remit and do not receive operating funding. This qualification completes the picture set out in the response: the historic line maintains an hourly passenger service, but the trains that run on it are part of a service offering planned at federal level and managed by FFS.
This account thus supports the conclusion expressed by the State Council: the three reopenings are acknowledged, but are placed in specific conditions, linked to the bus network and the configuration of service along the mountain route. The Government presents them as an exception, not as sufficient justification for extending the same solution to Giornico. ## Rules, requests and cultural enhancement
### The scope of requests in Leventina
Apart from Ambrì-Piotta, Lavorgo and Bodio, the Government specifies that no formal discussions have been initiated regarding any further reopenings in Leventina. The response recalls only one recent request: that of the Municipality of Prato Leventina for the Rodi-Fiesso station. The request had been submitted as part of the objection to the 2021 public transport offering, an objection subsequently rejected by the Grand Council.
On the railway side, FFS Infrastruttura rules out adding further stops. The reasons given are twofold: railway operations and costs. The Government also specifies that the assessment takes into account, in particular, the requirements arising from the Federal Act on the Elimination of Disadvantages for People with Disabilities. In the response, the reopening of a stop is therefore linked to technical, operational, cost and accessibility requirements.
The response refers to complex legislation, especially the Railways Act and the Disability Act. For technical matters, it identifies the website of the Federal Office of Transport as a reference. The timetable is an additional constraint: a new stop must not undermine the stability of planning, which is conditioned by constraints along the route and at important nodes such as Bellinzona.
The service under consideration is also the IR Locarno-Zurich/Basel, and therefore long-distance traffic. The Government points to the need to maintain attractive travel times: each stop penalizes through passengers, while the stops essential for transfers to road services must be retained. The response thus places timetable stability, journey duration and connections with road services on the same level.
The parliamentary question ultimately linked transport, culture and tourism. The topics mentioned included the findings of the Metron study on AlpTransit and Giornico's potential as an open-air museum. In its response, the State Council cites the continued existence of the mountain line, the return of service to the Ambrì-Piotta, Lavorgo and Bodio stops, and more effective integration with the bus network. According to the Executive, these elements brought a substantial improvement in public transport to Leventina, both qualitatively and quantitatively, with a network described as high-performing.
The picture presented therefore keeps two levels distinct: on the one hand, the historical and cultural enhancement requested for Giornico; on the other, the railway requirements that the Government considers binding for new stops. The source does not indicate formal negotiations to reopen Giornico; the reported outcome remains the abandonment of the study and the assessment that reopening is not justified.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/ticino/politica/1960171/linea-giornico-consiglio-fermata-fermate-riapertura-stato-ffs-stazione-apertura)*

## TL;DR - The assembly meets in Mendrisio on 10 November - Annual increases requested: from 5'159 to 8'941 francs - Reclassification: grades 4→5 and 5→6 - OCST and VPOD are also calling for cost-of-living compensation
## Key facts - What → reclassify OSC nursing staff - Who → OCST, VPOD and the Staff Committee - When → Tuesday, November 10, at 14.30 - Where → Mendrisio - Amount → between 5'159 and 8'941 francs annually - Origin → reclassification formally established in 2019 - Last formal request → January 2026
On October 30, 2026, the OCST and VPOD trade unions announced a new mobilization together with the Staff Committee. The appointment is set for Tuesday, November 10, at 14.30, in Mendrisio, with an agenda focused on salary demands and recovering the cost of living in the cantonal social and healthcare sector.
At the center is the nursing staff of the Cantonal Socio-Psychiatric Organization, the OSC. The organizations are calling for its reclassification and recovery of the cost of living, arguing that the salary adjustment has been stalled for years.
According to OCST and VPOD, the reclassification would entail annual increases ranging from 5'159 to 8'941 francs, depending on the position held. This concerns the economic aspect of the demand, while the classification aspect concerns moving to a different salary grade.
For nurses, the request provides for moving from grade 4 to grade 5. For nurses with specializations, the proposed move is from grade 5 to grade 6. The Joint Commission formally established this reclassification in 2019.
The unions link the recognition to the training, skills and responsibilities required in the cantonal socio-psychiatric context. In their view, the adjustment could also make the profession more attractive.
The political point of the mobilization is that the decision was never implemented. The report therefore concerns a demand that remains open, not an increase that has already been applied: the Government continues to oppose it for financial reasons and, according to the trade union organizations, confirmed this position at the latest meeting devoted to the issue.
For those looking at work in Canton Ticino from across the border, the documented fact is a wage dispute in a cantonal socio-psychiatric facility. However, the source does not indicate how many workers are involved or distinguish between residents and cross-border workers. ## From recognition to the dispute
The relationship between the 2019 decision and the situation described in 2026 provides the clearest comparison of the matter. The Joint Commission had formally approved the reclassification, but the change had not been implemented. In factual terms, therefore, the text distinguishes between the point at which the social partners recognized the grade change and the still-unrealized salary adjustment.
### Stages of the dispute
| Period | Documented element | |---|---| | 2019 | The Joint Commission approves the reclassification | | June 2022 | OCST, VPOD and the Staff Commission submit a petition | | January 2026 | The latest formal request is submitted to the Council of State | | Last meeting | According to the unions, the Government confirms its opposition for financial reasons | | 10 November | The Mendrisio assembly discusses the situation and possible actions |
The sequence also makes the shift from the decision to mobilization clear. After the 2019 ruling, the trade union organizations say they used a petition, public statements and formal requests. The latest of these dates to January 2026; the November meeting therefore follows a series of initiatives already listed in the source.
The amounts requested should be considered separately from the classification. The report indicates annual increases ranging from 5'159 to 8'941 francs, with the amount linked to the position held, without assigning either of the two values to a specific profile in the text. The arithmetic difference between the two extremes is 3'782 francs per year. The calculation uses only the figures given and does not establish which position corresponds to the minimum or the maximum.
The text also distinguishes between the two grade changes: from 4 to 5 for nurses and from 5 to 6 for those with a specialty. No other levels are indicated, nor is an implementation schedule described. For anyone working in Canton Ticino, including any cross-border commuter, the verifiable fact therefore remains the salary claim made by OSC. The source does not quantify the effect on an individual payslip and does not document the outcome of the political debate beyond confirming the Government's position. ## Cost of living and scope of the report
### A broader mobilization
The Mendrisio assembly will not be devoted solely to nurses of the Cantonal Socio-Psychiatric Organization. The recovery of the cost of living for public, para-public and social and healthcare staff is also among the topics of the meeting.
The second topic broadens the scope of the mobilization beyond the sole reclassification of the OSC. OCST and VPOD are calling for measures to protect purchasing power, while the claim concerning nurses relates to recognition of duties and responsibilities through the salary grades.
The report also states that, according to the unions, the request remains blocked by the cantonal budget as well. The organizations describe the failure to make the adjustment as a “long-standing freeze” and have decided to relaunch the mobilization following what they regard as a new refusal by the Government.
### What the text does not quantify
For readers who are cross-border commuters, the connection with cross-border work remains limited to salary matters in the Canton of Ticino. The text refers to OSC staff and the cantonal social and healthcare sector, but does not specify how many employees are cross-border commuters and does not document differences between those who reside in Switzerland and those who come from Italy.
Nor does it contain any information about an individual payslip, deductions or other social security and tax-related elements. For this reason, the annual amounts indicated by the unions cannot be converted into a personal net impact based solely on the article.
### No outcome announced in advance
The notice has a specific purpose: to take stock of the situation and discuss possible actions to support the pay claim. The source does not indicate which initiatives will be chosen, nor does it report an agreement with the Government or a date for implementing the reclassification.
The documented account therefore goes no further than the positions of the parties: the Joint Commission had approved the transition in 2019; OCST, VPOD and the Staff Commission had launched subsequent initiatives; the Government continues to oppose it for financial reasons, according to the unions; the Mendrisio assembly will now discuss developments.

item.description: Tax and social security guide for those who live in Brunate and work in Ticino, covering the new Cross-Border Agreement, withholding tax, exemptions
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Cross-Border Agreement in force from January 1st, 2024 - Old cross-border workers remain taxed only in Switzerland ([Art. 9 of the 2020 Agreement](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/it)). - For Article 9 of the Agreement, “old frontier workers” are people who met the tax requirements and worked in Graubünden, Ticino or Valais on 17 July 2023 or during the period from 31 December 2018 through 17 July 2023. Article 9 keeps covered employment income taxable exclusively at source in Switzerland; other workers follow the ordinary regime, with ordinary taxation in Italy, a credit for Swiss tax and Swiss withholding at 80% of the ordinary rates. The €10,000 figure in Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 is only the income limit referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013; it is not a general allowance for new frontier workers. Sources: [ESTV factsheet (Italian)](https://www.estv.admin.ch/dam/it/sd-web/Zbr5Jb-40aYm/int-laender-it-faktenblatt-faqs-it.pdf) · [Agreement, Art. 9](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/en) · [Law No. 83/2023, Art. 4](https://www.normattiva.it/atto/caricaDettaglioAtto?atto.articolo.numero=4&atto.codiceRedazionale=23G00087&atto.dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=2023-06-30&bloccoAggiornamentoBreadCrumb=true&classica=true&dataVigenza=09%2F09%2F2026&generaTabId=true&tipoDettaglio=singolavigenza&title=lbl.dettaglioAtto). - Withholding tax deducted in Switzerland
## Key facts - Agreement signing → December 23, 2020 - Entry into force → January 1, 2024 - Italian ratification → Law 83 of June 13, 2023 - Old cross-border workers remain taxed only in Switzerland (Art. 9 of the 2020 Agreement). - The €10,000 limit is not a general allowance: Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 applies it only to the income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013. - Convention → signed on March 9, 1976 - Double taxation → tax credit in section CE of the 730 form
The new Cross-Border Workers Agreement was signed on December 23, 2020 and entered into force on January 1, 2024. For those considering living in Brunate and working in Ticino as a cross-border worker, these two dates are the starting point for understanding the applicable tax treatment. The Italian ratification is Law 83 of June 13, 2023.
### The distinction that changes the tax framework
The date that separates the two regimes is July 17, 2023. The €10,000 limit is not a general allowance: Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 applies it only to the income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013. The stated criterion is the worker's status in relation to July 17, 2023, not merely the place of residence.
The rule concerning the payslip is equally clear: for cross-border workers, withholding tax on employment income is withheld in Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit reported in section CE of the 730 form. Therefore, when assessing the move to Brunate, the comparison should not be constructed by automatically adding a Swiss tax and an Italian tax on the same income. The source links the Italian mechanism to the tax credit, not to a second withholding.
The bilateral framework also includes the Convention for the avoidance of double taxation between Italy and Switzerland, signed on March 9, 1976. Switzerland is not a member of the European Union or the European Economic Area: this element too forms part of the framework within which the G permit, taxation and cross-border employment should be understood. The point is not to assign a special rule to Brunate, but to apply the cross-border-worker regime correctly to the individual situation.
Read in sequence, the chronology distinguishes three stages: signing on December 23, 2020, Italian ratification through Law 83 of June 13, 2023, and application from January 1, 2024. The date of July 17, 2023, on the other hand, is used to identify existing and new cross-border workers. ## From the payslip to coverage
The net income of a cross-border worker does not correspond to withholding tax. The rules set out here list separate Swiss contributions, and this separation is useful for those comparing work in Ticino with the choice of where to live in Brunate. The percentages provided should be read as separate items, without turning them into a personalized calculation of net income.
### The Swiss items listed
| Item | Documented data | | --- | --- | | AVS/AI/IPG | 5,3% paid by the employee | | AD/AC | 1,1%; cap CHF 148'200 | | LAINF | 0,7–1,5% | | LPP | 7–18% by age group, starting at age 25 |
AVS, AI and IPG are presented together with a combined rate of 5,3% for the employee. For AD/AC, the source indicates 1,1% and the limit of CHF 148'200. LAINF is reported with a range from 0,7% to 1,5%, while LPP varies from 7% to 18% based on age group, starting at age 25. These items belong to the contribution component, whereas withholding tax belongs to the tax component.
Health insurance also follows a separate logic. LAMal is health insurance, not a health tax; cross-border workers with a G permit have the right to choose. For adults, the indicated deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2'500. The right to choose is therefore an element to consider for a cross-border worker with a G permit, separate from contribution rates and taxation.
To keep income, social security and health coverage separate, you can consult page LAMal health insurance. The link concerns the health-related item; it does not replace the payslip data or modify the rates listed. When comparing living in Brunate and working in Ticino, the usable information is therefore the structure of the items: AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF and LPP on the one hand; withholding tax and LAMal on the other. ## Figures for the Canton of Ticino and responsibilities
In the first quarter of 2026, USTAT counted 78'561 cross-border commuters in Ticino, a slight decrease, equal to approximately 32% of employed persons. This is the territorial figure reported for the Canton of Ticino. For individual taxation, the distinction between those who were already cross-border commuters before July 17, 2023, and those who fall into the category of new cross-border commuters remains decisive.
### 2026 is not the date of the agreement
The USTAT figure for 2026 and the date of the new Cross-Border Commuters Agreement should not be conflated. The agreement entered into force on January 1, 2024, while the first quarter of 2026 is the statistical period. This distinction prevents attributing to 2026 an agreement that the source places in 2020 for its signing and in 2024 for its entry into force.
Institutional responsibility must also be interpreted precisely. Tax rates, including withholding tax and federal and cantonal rates, are established by federal and cantonal laws. At the federal level, the administration identified is AFC/ESTV, while the cantonal tax administrations are also involved. BFS collects statistical data: it does not set the rates. For its part, USTAT is the body cited for counting cross-border commuters in the first quarter of 2026.
For the Italian side, the source reports the 2026 IRPEF rates as 23% up to €28'000, 33% between €28'001 and €50'000, and 43% above €50'000, under Law 199/2025, Art. 1, para. 3. For 2024–2025 income, it instead indicates 23%, 35% and 43%. These figures remain distinct references within the Italian system and should not automatically be added to the Swiss withholding: for the cross-border commuter, employment income is subject to withholding tax in Switzerland, and Italy uses the tax credit in section CE of form 730.
As for the links, the editorial references mention Brogeda, Gaggiolo, A2/A9, the roads in Ticino and those in the provinces of Varese, Como and VCO, as well as TILO/FFS. The economic comparison between residence and work can be developed by separating the documented items from the rest; the relevant operational reference is cost of living in Ticino vs Italy.
Article 1(237–238) of Italian Law No. 213/2023 does not apply indiscriminately to all cross-border workers. It covers: (a) Italian residents who work and stay in Switzerland and use the Italian SSN; (b) frontier workers under Article 9(1) of the Italy–Switzerland Agreement whose income is taxable only in Switzerland and who exercised the legal right to choose health insurance; and (c) dependants of those two categories. Paragraph 238 sets a progressive 3–6% share of net Swiss salary, with a €30 minimum and an ordinary €200 maximum for each month worked from 2024. The cap may be doubled in cases of omitted payment or omitted communication specified in Article 1(100) of Law No. 207/2024. The Region of residence sets the rates and procedure each year.

## TL;DR - Cross-Border Workers Agreement in force from January 1st, 2024 - Old cross-border workers remain taxed only in Switzerland ([Art. 9 of the 2020 Agreement](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/it)). - For Article 9 of the Agreement, “old frontier workers” are people who met the tax requirements and worked in Graubünden, Ticino or Valais on 17 July 2023 or during the period from 31 December 2018 through 17 July 2023. Article 9 keeps covered employment income taxable exclusively at source in Switzerland; other workers follow the ordinary regime, with ordinary taxation in Italy, a credit for Swiss tax and Swiss withholding at 80% of the ordinary rates. The €10,000 figure in Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 is only the income limit referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013; it is not a general allowance for new frontier workers. Sources: [ESTV factsheet (Italian)](https://www.estv.admin.ch/dam/it/sd-web/Zbr5Jb-40aYm/int-laender-it-faktenblatt-faqs-it.pdf) · [Agreement, Art. 9](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/en) · [Law No. 83/2023, Art. 4](https://www.normattiva.it/atto/caricaDettaglioAtto?atto.articolo.numero=4&atto.codiceRedazionale=23G00087&atto.dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=2023-06-30&bloccoAggiornamentoBreadCrumb=true&classica=true&dataVigenza=09%2F09%2F2026&generaTabId=true&tipoDettaglio=singolavigenza&title=lbl.dettaglioAtto). - Canton Ticino: 78'561 cross-border workers in Q1 2026
## Key facts | Term | Value | |---|---| | Agreement | signed on December 23, 2020 | | Effective date | January 1st, 2024 | | Existing cross-border workers | €7'500; transitional 2024–2033 | The €10,000 limit is not a general allowance: Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 applies it only to the income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013. | Tax | withheld in Switzerland | | Credit | CE section of Form 730 | | Statistic | 78'561 in the first quarter of 2026 | | LAMal | adult deductible CHF 300–2'500 |
### The agreement timeline As of January 1st, 2024, the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement is in force. Signed on December 23, 2020, it was ratified in Italy by Law 83 of June 13, 2023. For anyone considering living in Arcisate and working in Ticino as a cross-border worker, the basic tax rule is clear. Withholding on the cross-border worker's employment income takes place in Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit provided for in the CE section of Form 730. The issue therefore concerns withholding tax and cannot be understood as double Italian-Swiss withholding.
### Existing and new cross-border workers The timeline is not enough: the definition of the two categories also matters. The €10,000 limit is not a general allowance: Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 applies it only to the income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013. These are different values and periods and should not be combined into a single threshold.
The framework is based on the Convention for the Avoidance of Double Taxation between Italy and Switzerland, signed on March 9, 1976. Switzerland is not a member of the EU or the EEA: work in Canton Ticino must therefore be understood within a bilateral tax relationship, not as an ordinary movement of work within the Union.
The logistical aspect remains distinct from the tax aspect. Connections, travel times and border crossings are part of the housing choice, but referring to a crossing such as Brogeda does not by itself make it possible to assign a duration to the journey from Arcisate. For this reason, the practical figure must be verified separately, including via border crossing wait times, without turning a general assessment into an individual figure. ## The economic comparison The economic advantage of living in Arcisate and working in Ticino cannot be measured by a single figure. Tax withholding is one item, while the payslip includes Swiss contributions stated with different percentages, caps, and age brackets. A useful comparison requires keeping these bases separate, without automatically adding up values presented in different forms.
### Swiss contributions The contribution table clarifies which elements affect the pay framework:
| Item | Stated figure | |---|---| | AVS/AI/IPG | 5.3% paid by the employee | | AD/AC | 1.1%, with a CHF 148'200 cap | | LAINF | 0.7–1.5% | | LPP | 7–18% by age bracket, starting at age 25 |
These items explain why net income cannot be reconstructed using only the tax rate. AVS/AI/IPG is stated as an employee contribution; AD/AC is subject to the CHF 148'200 limit; LPP varies by age bracket starting at age 25. The LAINF figure, by contrast, is provided as a 0.7–1.5% range. Each item must therefore be read according to its own unit and criterion.
### The comparison with IRPEF Italian legislation also distinguishes tax rates over time. From 2026, under Law 199/2025, Article 1, paragraph 3, IRPEF is 23% up to €28'000, 33% between €28'001 and €50'000, and 43% above €50'000. For income in 2024–2025, the rates indicated are instead 23%, 35%, and 43%.
These brackets describe the Italian IRPEF framework; they do not override the specific rule for cross-border workers, namely withholding in Switzerland and a tax credit to avoid double taxation. The cost of living must also be considered separately. Tax rates and contributions alone do not measure the cost of housing, mobility, or daily expenses associated with relocation. For this reason, the comparison between Arcisate and Ticino must set housing costs alongside the tax framework, using cost of living in Ticino vs Italy without turning a general parameter into a monthly amount applicable to every cross-border worker. ## G permit, healthcare and data on Canton Ticino The move is not limited to the relationship between salary and tax. The framework to consider includes the G permit, social security and health insurance, while statistics describe the overall scale of cross-border employment in Canton Ticino. These are areas connected to the decision, but they are not interchangeable.
### LAMal and G permit LAMal is health insurance. Cross-border workers with a G permit have the right of option and, for adults, the specified deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2'500. This figure defines a healthcare component of the comparison. It is not equivalent to an income tax rate and does not, by itself, alter the withholding tax rule.
### Data and responsibilities In the first quarter of 2026 USTAT records 78'561 cross-border workers in Canton Ticino, a slight decrease representing approximately 32% of employed persons. This is an overall territorial figure: it does not make it possible to convert the cantonal statistic into a figure referring to Arcisate, nor to infer an economic advantage for someone changing residence from it alone.
To understand whom to contact, the area must be distinguished: federal and cantonal withholding tax rates are established by the applicable laws and administered, respectively, by AFC/ESTV at the federal level and by the cantonal tax administrations. Social security, including the AVS/AI area, instead falls within the remit of UFAS; BFS is limited to collecting statistical data. Consequently, neither UFAS nor BFS determines tax rates.
This distinction helps assess advantages and disadvantages without oversimplifying them. The tax credit documents the mechanism for preventing double taxation; the G permit and LAMal belong to other areas; the commute and cost of living require a separate assessment. To organize the tax and remuneration items of the move, tax calculator can be used.

## TL;DR - At Gaggiolo, a driver entered Italy - A high-end bag and scarf found in the trunk - The undeclared items are worth more than 23.000 euros
## Key facts - Location → Gaggiolo - Direction → entering Italy - Subject → a female driver - Declaration → nothing to declare - Discovery → a high-end handbag and scarf - Value → over 23,000 euros
In Gaggiolo, a female driver entering Italy declared that she had nothing to declare. However, a high-end handbag and scarf were found in the trunk, described by the source as undeclared items worth more than 23,000 euros.
### The sequence of the case The central point of the report is the contrast between what the driver stated and what was found in the trunk. The source does not identify the person, indicate her profession, or link the crossing to a business trip. It only describes entry into Italy and the discovery of the two items.
The reported value is expressed as an amount exceeding 23,000 euros. The precise amount is not indicated, nor is it divided between the handbag and the scarf. For this reason too, the report allows the contents of the inspection to be reconstructed, but not an exact price to be assigned to the individual objects. ## The value is not an exact figure The strongest comparison that emerges from the text does not concern two prices, but two different pieces of information: on the one hand, the driver's declaration, and on the other, the discovery of the items in the trunk. The source reports that the driver had nothing to declare, while the headline describes the items as undeclared.
### What the number indicates The phrase more than 23.000 euros indicates a minimum threshold for the total value attributed to the items. Writing that the bag is worth a specific amount, or that the scarf is worth the remaining amount, would go beyond the available data. Both the separate price of the two goods and a precise final figure are missing.
The same limitation applies to any possible financial consequences. The material provided does not indicate a penalty, quantify any amounts owed, or explain which criterion was applied to the value of the items. The reported number therefore serves to describe the order of magnitude of the discovery, not to calculate an administrative amount.
For anyone crossing the border on entry into Italy, the documented fact therefore remains limited to this episode: a declaration followed by the discovery of high-end goods. It is not a report about salaries, pay slips, or taxation. ## The limits of the available information The material provided does not identify the driver, indicate her place of residence, or specify where she came from before entering Italy. Nor does it say whether the trip was work-related or whether the person was a cross-border worker. The connection with a professional category, therefore, cannot be inferred from the case.
The source also does not specify the authority that carried out the inspection, the date of the incident, the commercial origin of the bag and scarf, or their separate price. The subsequent administrative handling of the matter is not reported either. The available text only allows us to state that two undeclared high-end items were found in the trunk, worth more than 23.000 euros.
There are no references to a G permit, AVS, LPP, LAMal, withholding tax, tax rebates, or double taxation. These elements are not connected to the incident by the source and cannot be added to turn a border report into a report about cross-border work. The publication date and time are also not part of the available original text.

item.description: Malnate will receive almost 500,000 euros less in refreshes this year than last year.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Malnate will receive almost 500 thousand euros less - The national fund goes from 89 to 108 million - Refreshments will arrive in early November - Nearly 1,700 Malnatesi cross the border every day
## Key facts - → Borderers' refreshments - Place → Malnate - → Almost 500 thousand euros less than last year - National Fund → from 89 to 108 million - Times → usually June; thisyear in early November
### The figure for Malnate Malnate will receive almost 500,000 euros less in refreshes this year than last year. According to what Malpensa24 reported, the mayor Nadia Cannito intervened on the issue, considering these resources relevant for a municipality such as hers.
Border workers' allowances correspond to the part of the tax revenue paid in Switzerland by cross-border workers that is returned to the municipalities in which they reside. The sums are intended to finance services and public works. The issue therefore affects the resources of the municipal administrations, but the source does not specify the total amount allocated to Malnate.
> The mayor explains that those resources are linked to the work of almost 1,700 malnatesi, who cross the border daily.
Cannito highlights the link between the restaurants and the work of the residents of Malnate who cross the border every day. He also highlights that the national fund has gone from 89 to 108 million, recognizing the role played by the organization that brings together the Italian border municipalities and its president Massimo Mastromarino, whom he thanks.
The association, according to the mayor, has also committed itself to keeping the distribution criteria as close as possible to those used so far. It also asked the Region to send communications on the sums to the Municipalities without waiting for the opinion of the Budgetary Control Office, because such communications already have the value of a legal obligation.
However, the total remains lower than that required by the border municipalities. Deadlines also create difficulties: normally refunds are credited in June, while thisyear they will be included in the last budget change, scheduled for early November. Malnate will therefore only have a few weeks to plan and use resources for planning the entire year. ## From the national fund to the municipal share
The comparison between the data reported by the mayor highlights two different levels: on the one hand the national fund, on the other the concrete availability for the Municipality of Malnate. The source reports that the former went from 89 to 108 million. The arithmetic difference between the two values ​​is 19 million, but the text does not indicate which share of this fund is assigned to each Municipality.
| Voice | Data available | |---|---| | National Fund | from 89 to 108 million | | Arithmetic difference | 19 million | | Result for Malnate | almost 500 thousand euros less than last year | | Usual arrival | June | | Arrival indicated for this year | in early November |
This comparison does not allow the growth of the national fund to be transformed into an estimate of the sum allocated to Malnate. The news does not provide either the total amount due to the Municipality or a percentage of distribution. Instead, it reports the political-administrative data highlighted by Cannito: the fund has increased, but the amount allocated to Malnate remains lower than what the border municipalities asked for.
The reference to the almost 1,700 Malnatese also has a precise meaning. The mayor uses it to link the refunds to the work of those who cross the border every day; However, a calculation for each cross-border worker is not indicated, nor an individual sum. The mechanism described concerns the return of taxes paid in Switzerland to the municipalities of residence and the subsequent destination for public services and works.
### Criteria and calendar
The position of the Association of Italian Border Municipalities also concerns the method. The objective indicated by Cannito is to keep the distribution criteria close to those used so far, while regional communications on the sums should reach the Municipalities without waiting for the opinion of the Budget Control Office. The source attributes to those communications the value of an already acquired legal obligation.
The calendar remains separate from the fund value. The usual arrival in June and the one expected in early November are the two available time references. A precise date for the accreditation is not indicated, but the mayor points out that the inclusion in the latest budget change leaves a few weeks to plan the use of the resources. ## The political sticking point between Lombardy and Canton Ticino
The most delicate issue concerns the dispute between the Lombardy Region and Canton Ticino. Cannito argues that, just when the border municipalities were seeking stability, the Lombardy Region extended the healthcare levy introduced by the Government, the health tax, to legacy cross-border workers. According to the mayor, this decision triggered the clash with Canton Ticino.
The suspension dates back to June: Ticino withheld half of the rebates intended for Lombardy. Piedmont, which chose not to apply the health tax, did not suffer any blockage. The source compares the two Regions but does not state the value in euros of Lombardy’s suspended share.
Cannito calls these decisions political and warns that the border municipalities risk paying the price. Her request to the Region is to withdraw the health tax; she asks the Government instead to guarantee the border municipalities all the resources due to them, with certain timing every year.
For Malnate, the mayor assures that every euro received will be allocated to services and works. The reported problem therefore does not concern a different allocation of the funds, but the possibility of knowing their amount and availability sufficiently in advance to plan the municipal budget.
The source does not state the total rebates due to Malnate, nor does it quantify the effect of the regional suspension on the individual municipality. Nor does it report any individual impact on the nearly 1,700 people from Malnate who cross the border every day. The available figure remains the administrative one: nearly 500,000 euros less than last year, against a national fund that rose from 89 to 108 million and an expected arrival in early November.
The affair thus shows a difference between the national dimension of the fund, regional decisions, and the planning of municipalities of residence. To follow the issue of transfers between Switzerland and Italian municipalities, consult the page on Ticino-Italy tax rebates.

The clarification on the audience is a central part of the news: the source does not present the phrase as referred indiscriminately to every cross-border worker and does not describe other categories.
The title accompanies the motion with a threat of blocking reimbursements by Ticino. The text does not indicate a date, a procedure, or conditions for a possible block. item.description: Malnate will receive almost 500 thousand euros less in rebates.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR
- Malnate will receive almost 500 thousand euros less in rebates. - Almost 1.700 residents cross the border every day. - The funds will arrive in early November, not in June. - The mayor is calling for certainty and the withdrawal of the healthcare tax.
| Item | Value | |---|---| | Municipality | Malnate | | Resident workers | Almost 1.700 | | Expected reduction | Almost 500 thousand euros | | National fund | From 89 to 108 million | | Usual payment | June | | Indicated payment | Early November | | Mayor | Nadia Cannito | | Institutional dispute | Regione Lombardia and Canton Ticino |
For Malnate, rebates for cross-border workers will be almost 500 thousand euros lower than last year. VareseNews reports that almost 1.700 workers who cross the Swiss border every day live in the municipality. Mayor Nadia Cannito has raised the issue of the cut, the timing of disbursement, and tensions between Regione Lombardia and Canton Ticino.
### The amount and the schedule
The rebates consist of returning to municipalities of residence a portion of the taxes paid in Switzerland by cross-border workers. According to the account reported by the source, these resources finance public works and essential services. For Malnate, the issue therefore concerns both the amount available and the time available to include it in municipal planning.
In the statement, the mayor links the fund to the work of almost 1.700 residents of Malnate. She then emphasizes that the national allocation has risen from 89 to 108 million, also thanks to the Associazione dei Comuni italiani di frontiera and its president Massimo Mastromarino, whom she thanks. The association worked to keep the allocation criteria as close as possible to those used so far and asked the Region to send municipalities notifications of the amounts.
However, the amount remains lower than that requested by the border municipalities, leaving Malnate with a shortfall of almost 500 thousand euros. The issue is not merely accounting-related: the payment, normally scheduled for June, will be included in the final budget amendment in early November this year. According to Cannito, only a few weeks will remain to plan and carefully use resources that should serve to plan the entire year. ## Rebates and budget: what the data show
Malnate’s figure can be understood by comparing the origin, destination, amount and timing of the rebates. The source does not refer to a sum allocated to each worker, but to resources that return to the municipalities where the workers reside after cross-border workers pay taxes in Switzerland.
### Two aspects not to be confused
| Dimension | Data reported by the source | |---|---| | Origin | Share of the taxes paid in Switzerland by cross-border workers | | Destination | Public works and essential services in the municipalities where they reside | | National fund | From 89 to 108 million | | Malnate’s share | Almost 500 thousand euros less than last year | | Timing | From June to early November |
The first comparison is between the national fund and the municipal share. The fund increased from 89 to 108 million, but the statement nonetheless reports a reduction of almost 500 thousand euros for Malnate. The two figures describe different levels: one concerns the overall allocation indicated by the mayor, while the other concerns the amount earmarked for a single municipality. The source does not provide the full breakdown and does not allow the case of Malnate to be automatically extended to all border municipalities.
The second comparison concerns timing. The usual crediting in June and the expected crediting in early November are the two deadlines being compared. For the municipal administration, the delay reduces the weeks available to include the resources in the budget adjustment, plan the projects and use the funds within a one-year period.
For an individual cross-border worker, therefore, the text documents the passage through the budget of the municipality where they reside, not a change in their payslip. No basis is provided for calculating how much of the reduction would correspond to each worker. ## The dispute between the Lombardy Region and Canton Ticino
According to Mayor Nadia Cannito, the political issue stems from the Region's decision to subject old cross-border workers to the health tax introduced by the Government. The decision, the mayor reports, triggered a dispute with Canton Ticino and had repercussions for the payments allocated to Lombardy.
### The June suspension
In June, Ticino suspended half of the payments intended for Lombardy. The comparison reported by the mayor also concerns Piedmont: because it did not apply the tax, according to the account contained in the source, it did not suffer any suspension. Cannito describes these decisions as political and argues that the risk falls on border municipalities, which are called upon to organize services and public works with resources that arrive later and in smaller amounts than expected.
However, the source does not provide a breakdown of Malnate's shortfall. It does not indicate which part of the nearly 500 thousand euros is attributable to the suspension of Lombardy's payments and which instead depends on allocation criteria or the other factors mentioned in the statement. Nor does it report a schedule other than early November for the expected payment, or a list of municipal projects that could be postponed.
### The requests and limitations of the report
Cannito urges the Region to repeal the health tax and restore relations with Ticino. She asks the Government to guarantee border municipalities all the resources they are entitled to, with definite timing each year. The only stated destination for the funds that will arrive is general: services and public works for Malnate.
It is therefore not possible to infer from the statement any individual effects in these areas or to automatically link the municipal cut to a cross-border worker's pension, insurance or administrative status. To follow the issue of resources between the two territories, consult Ticino-Italy tax rebates.

## Key facts - Location: Chiasso - Structure: federal asylum center - Employment situation: 28 people without work - Area concerned: via Motta - Indicated timeframe: until mid-2027 - Subsequent criterion: number of applications - Person mentioned: Raffaele De Rosa - Source of information: SEM
In Chiasso, the closure of via Motta affects 28 people without work. This is the central figure reported by the source, which also indicates in the same update the future of the federal asylum center: it will not reopen before mid-2027.
Raffaele De Rosa, informed by SEM, said that the center will remain closed until that deadline. The text does not provide a specific date, but indicates mid-2027 as the point before which the center will not reopen. It therefore does not announce an immediate reopening or provide a more detailed schedule.
### The decision deferred until after mid-2027
After that deadline, the situation will be assessed based on the number of applications. The criterion mentioned therefore concerns the number of applications, while the source provides neither their number nor a threshold already established for making the decision. The news thus brings together two distinct elements: the employment figure of 28 people without work and the future assessment of the center’s operations.
Regarding employment in Canton Ticino, the case remains limited to Chiasso and the figures explicitly reported. The source provides no information about other facilities, other municipalities or additional jobs affected. It also does not specify whether the 28 people are employees of the center or have another connection to the closure of via Motta. These limitations prevent the figure from being turned into a broader snapshot of employment in the Mendrisiotto. ## What can be compared
The available data allow a comparison between the employment outlook and the time frame, but not between two statistical series. On the one hand, there is the absolute number of people without work; on the other, there is a deadline indicated for the federal asylum centre. These are different types of information, and the source provides no other figures with which to calculate changes, percentages or differences.
| Element | Reported data | |---|---| | People without work | 28 | | Centre | federal asylum centre | | Reopening | not until mid-2027 | | Subsequent assessment | number of applications |
The table makes visible the relationship between what has already been described and what remains subject to an assessment. The 28 people represent the employment figure indicated in the news headline. Mid-2027, however, is not presented as the date of a definite reopening: until then, the centre will not reopen, while afterwards a decision will be made based on the number of applications.
### The limit for cross-border commuters
For a cross-border commuter reading the news in relation to employment in Ticino, the information gap is clear: the text documents an employment case in Chiasso, but does not say how many of the 28 people are involved in cross-border commuting. Nor does it indicate contracts, duties, residence or any possible consequences for other workers. The number therefore cannot be interpreted as data about cross-border commuters in the Canton of Ticino.
The verifiable relationship remains that between via Motta, the 28 people without work and the federal asylum centre. The source does not describe changes in the number of applications, does not compare different periods and does not attribute the future assessment to another reason. For this reason, the useful comparison is primarily between the definitive employment figure concerned and the decision deferred until after mid-2027. ## What is not indicated
The report identifies an institutional source, SEM, and attributes the information to Raffaele De Rosa. Beyond these references, the text does not provide the name of a department, an operator or another authority involved. It does not indicate the start date of the closure, how long it has already lasted or the professional status of the 28 people.
The number of applications used as the basis for the subsequent assessment is also missing. Consequently, it cannot be established from the available data whether the centre will reopen after mid-2027: the source only says that it will not reopen until then and that the situation will subsequently be assessed based on the applications. This is the distinction between a communicated time limit and a future decision not yet described.
For the cross-border worker audience, the same caution applies to what the source does not address. It does not even mention INPS or tax rebates. These topics are not linked to the closure of via Motta, so they cannot be inferred from the announcement.
### The scope of the report
The scope therefore remains local: Chiasso, via Motta, the federal asylum centre and 28 people without work. The only development indicated is the subsequent assessment, linked to the number of applications. Without that figure and additional information about the people involved, any estimate of the impact on the Ticino labour market or on cross-border workers would go beyond the source.

item.title: Cross-border workers in Ticino: 55,6% feel they are paid less
item.description: A total of 1'542 cross-border workers took part in the survey presented today in Varese.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 1'542 workers responded to the survey - 73% satisfied with their salary - 55,6% feel they are paid less than a resident - 37,4% can work remotely
## Key facts - Sample → 1'542 workers - Organizers → BiblioLavoro, Cisl Lombardia and OCST - Presentation → Varese - Salary satisfaction → 73% - Pay compared with a resident → 55,6% - Reduced purchasing power → 48,4% - Teleworking possible → 37,4% - Impact of commuting → for many, between 5% and 20% of their paycheck
A total of 1'542 cross-border workers took part in the survey presented today in Varese. The survey was conducted jointly by BiblioLavoro, the research center of Cisl Lombardia, and OCST, the Ticino trade union. They are people who travel to work in Ticino every day.
The survey reveals a paradox: although they earn more than in Italy, more than half believe they are treated worse than their Swiss colleagues. 73% say they are satisfied with their salary; however, 55,6% think they earn less than a resident doing the same work. Moreover, almost half of respondents (48,4%) perceive a reduction in their purchasing power.
### The twofold signal on pay
The percentages do not refer to the same question. The 73% concerns satisfaction with salary, while the 55,6% concerns the comparison with a resident employed in the same role. The 48,4% adds the perception regarding purchasing power. Taken together, the three figures show that a positive assessment of the amount received can coexist with the belief that one is paid less than another worker and with the feeling of having less purchasing power.
The source does not indicate the participants' average salary and does not reconstruct the circumstances of individual cases. The survey therefore provides percentages referring to the sample of 1'542 responses. The report concerns the work of cross-border workers in the Canton of Ticino, but the text does not turn the aggregate data into a measure of every cross-border worker's pay. The salary comparison remains the one reported by the participants: the source reports a belief, not an individual calculation of the paycheck. Regarding commuting, the daily travel time exceeds an hour and a half for one third of cross-border workers, while nearly three quarters of them travel by car. For many, mobility costs account for between 5% and 20% of their pay packet. Working remotely could help, but only 37,4% have the possibility of doing so.
### Mobility and differences between women and men
| Indicator | Reported figure | |---|---| | Travel time | One in three cross-border workers over an hour and a half per day | | Mode of transport used | Nearly three in four by car | | Weight of mobility | Between 5% and 20% of their pay packet | | Remote work | 37,4% can do it | | Female workers earning under 3'000 gross francs | One quarter | | Men earning under 3'000 gross francs | 8,2% |
The table compares different indicators without adding them together. The 20% is the upper limit of the interval indicated for mobility, not an average applicable to all workers. Similarly, 37,4% measures the possibility of working remotely in the sample, while the source does not say how many days of remote work are possible.
The comparison between men and women is based on the share below a threshold: 25% of female workers receive less than 3'000 gross francs per month, while among men the percentage is 8,2%. Thus, two average salaries are not being compared, but rather the share of workers who remain below that monthly limit. The source documents the disparity, but does not explain its causes or indicate the numerical size of the groups of women and men. In the context of cross-border employment, the text places commuting, access to remote work and wage distribution alongside one another, without establishing a causal relationship between these elements. The move to Ticino does not emerge as a majority option. The idea appeals to only one in four; the source links the choice to the cost of living and health insurance premiums, as well as the distance from family. The text does not quantify these costs or assign them a separate figure.
### The union's request
Among the proposals, the union again calls for a status for cross-border workers that would provide greater certainty regarding taxation and social security. This is a request reported by the source, not a description of a measure that has already been approved. Marco Contessa, Cisl's national head of cross-border workers, said:
> “Cross-border workers are not privileged, but bridges between two countries”
The scope of the text is limited to pay, commuting, teleworking, differences between men and women, relocation and the union's request. Nor does it quantify tax rebates, withholding tax or double taxation. These topics therefore cannot be used to attribute to the survey conclusions that the text does not contain.
This is the extent of the available data: a snapshot of the responses collected in Varese, without historical series, comparisons with other surveys or subsequent results documented in the text. To calculate your own payslip, consult payslip simulator.

## TL;DR - 31.7% exceed one and a half hours per day - 73.2% use a private car - 28.3% spend more than 10% of salary - 37.4% have remote work
## Key facts - Search → "Working across borders" - Creation of → BiblioLavoro, CISL Lombardy study centre - Sample → 1,542 border workers; online questionnaire in May 2026 - Presentation → on Saturday 24 October at Ville Ponti, Varese - Teleworking tax threshold → 25%
The online questionnaire, which in May 2026 was answered by 1,542 border workers, most of whom are members of the OCST, finds that 31.7% spend more than an hour and a half a day on the journey between home and work. The investigation was presented on Saturday 24 October at Ville Ponti, in Varese.
The survey "Working beyond the border" was conducted by BiblioLavoro, a CISL Lombardy study centre, for CISL dei Laghi, CISL Sondrio, CISL Piemonte Orientale and the Ticino Ocst trade union. The costs of work in Ticino that do not appear in the paycheck also include travel: the time spent on the road and the money needed to travel it.
### The daily time dedicated to the journey
In the daily round trip, only 12.5% of respondents stay under 30 minutes; 30% are between 30 and 60 minutes and 25.8% between 60 and 90. For 31.7%, on the other hand, the journey exceeds one and a half hours: 14.6% takes from 91 to 120 minutes, 17.1% more than two hours and 3.2% more than three hours.
The weekly frequency makes the figure even more concrete. 66.1% of border crossers make this trip five days a week; another 27.2% make it four days. Combining duration and frequency allows you to read the results on two scales: the time declared on a round trip and the days of the week on which the journey is repeated. The research keeps the bands separate and does not offer a single average time; therefore 12.5% under half anhour and 31.7% over an hour and a half remain two distinct groups, not extremes of a calculated average.
> Marco Contessa, national head of Frontiers of the CISL, observed that economic motivation continues to attract workers, while daily commuting and the heavy costs of mobility feed a real "time trap". The data on travel time translates into a choice of mobility and a portion of the monthly salary allocated to travel. The research separates the two levels: first it measures the main means of transport, then the salary range absorbed by the trip. The comparison is useful precisely because it does not automatically attribute a single expense to each vehicle.
### Car-centric commuting
| Main medium | Share of respondents | |---|---:| | Private car | 73.2% | | Train | 10.5% | | Motorcycles and scooters | 6% | | More means | 3.8% | | Company car | 3.4% | | Carpooling | 2.6% | | Bus | 0.5% |
The private car is the main means of transport for 73.2% of those interviewed, a significantly higher share than the train, which stands at 10.5%. Motorcycles and scooters reach 6%, while 3.8% combine multiple vehicles. The company car is indicated by 3.4%, car pooling by 2.6% and the bus by 0.5%.
The authors of the research also attribute this distribution to the limits of the cross-border public transport offer; the use of cars exposes workers to traffic and waiting at border crossings. The text does not indicate specific crossings or quantify expectations: the documented data concerns the composition of the vehicles used by cross-border workers.
### Spending as a share of salary
| Share of monthly salary | Interviewees | |---|---:| | Between 5% and 10% | 47.7% | | Between 10% and 20% | 21.6% | | Over 20% | 6.6% |
Travel expenses affect the monthly salary between 5% and 10% for 47.7% of those interviewed; for 21.6% the share is between 10% and 20%, while 6.6% exceeds 20%. Overall, for 28.3% of those interviewed, travel absorbs more than 10% of the salary, i.e. more than a tenth of the salary.
The comparison between public and private methods concerns the same share of the salary: 32.2% of those who use public transport remain under 5%, compared to 19.7% of those who travel by private means. The difference is 12.5 percentage points, calculated as 32.2% minus 19.7%. The presentation keeps the two indicators distinct: 28.3% concerns the expenditure relating to the salary, while 73.2% concerns the used vehicle. Research links work from home to business readiness, contribution regime, and tax threshold. Only 37.4% of respondents work in companies that allow border workers to work remotely; when this possibility is provided, in 92.5% of cases it remains limited to a share between 10% and 25% of the time.
95.2% of those who use work from home rate its impact on quality of life positively, while 94.3% would like to use it for more days. The reasons most often given are better work-life balance (42.5%), less time spent travelling (42.4%), less travel-related stress (34.7%) and lower transport costs (33.7%).
### Two thresholds for the same work-from-home job
The constraint does not depend only on companies. The European agreement on cross-border teleworking, signed by Italy and Switzerland, allows a border worker to work from home up to 49.99% of the time without changing the contribution regime. On the fiscal side, however, the agreement between Italy and Switzerland sets the threshold at 25%.
According to the reconstruction proposed by the research, in the negotiation Switzerland was willing to reach 40%, as it had done with France; the Italian position, however, raised the tax threshold to 25%. The union proposes to reopen the additional protocol to align both thresholds at 49.99% or, at least, to raise the tax threshold to 40%. The difference between 49.99% and 25% therefore concerns the two thresholds cited by the source: the first for contributions, the second for tax.
### Satisfaction and duration of the trip
The work-life balance leaves 44.2% of respondents with little or no satisfaction, a percentage that reaches 49.9% among those under 36. Satisfaction concerns 69.5% of those who also work from home and 51.8% of those who work exclusively in person. The questionnaire therefore finds a distance of 17.7 percentage points between the two groups; among those under 36, on the other hand, the proportion of those little or not at all satisfied is 5.7 points higher than the total.
The researchers' statistical analysis confirms a relationship: all other things being equal, job satisfaction decreases the longer the daily commute. The source adds neither a single average time nor an individual threshold.
### The perimeter of the data
For the border crossing of the Canton of Ticino, the questionnaire described here does not measure G, AVS, LPP, LAMal, REFORNI, INPS, tax at source or double taxation: these issues are not quantified in the results reported. The fiscal reference of the search remains the threshold of teleworking.
To deepen the mobility side, the comparison can continue with the Ticino public transport.
*Source: [varesenews.it](https://www.varesenews.it/2026/10/un-frontaliere-su-tre-passa-piu-di-unora-e-mezza-al-giorno-in-viaggio/2718007/)*

item.title: Gender pay disparity among cross-border workers in Ticino
item.description: On Saturday, October 24, the results of «Working across borders» were presented at Ville Ponti in Varese.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Online research in May 2026 involving 1.542 cross-border workers - Women make up 42,4% of the sample - Under 3.500 francs: 41,5% of female cross-border workers - Under equal conditions, approximately 520 more gross francs for men
## Key facts Research → «Working across borders» Conducted by → BiblioLavoro, research center of Cisl Lombardia Questionnaire → online in May 2026 Sample → 1.542 cross-border workers, mostly members of Ocst Presentation → Saturday, October 24, Ville Ponti, Varese Women in the sample → 42,4%
On Saturday, October 24, the results of «Working across borders» were presented at Ville Ponti in Varese. BiblioLavoro, the research center of Cisl Lombardia, conducted the survey for Cisl dei Laghi, Cisl Sondrio, Cisl Piemonte Orientale and the Ticino trade union Ocst, based on an online questionnaire to which, in May 2026, 1.542 cross-border workers responded, most of them members of Ocst.
### The basis for comparison
Women account for 38,5% of Italians working in Ticino; in the province of Varese, female cross-border workers number 12.164, accounting for 39% of the total. In the research sample, the female share rises to 42,4%. The percentages refer to different bases: the first to Italians employed in Ticino, the second to female cross-border workers in the province of Varese, and the third to the people who answered the questionnaire. From a purely arithmetic standpoint, the sample is 3,9 points higher than 38,5% and 3,4 points higher than 39%.
### Income brackets The difference becomes more evident when looking at the monthly gross income shares reported by the research.
| Monthly gross income | Female cross-border workers | Men | |---|---:|---:| | Less than 2.500 francs | 13,4% | 2,6% | | Less than 3.000 francs | 25,4% | 8,2% | | Less than 3.500 francs | 41,5% | 17,4% | | At least 5.000 francs | 22,2% | 41,1% |
The differences between the shares are 10,8 percentage points below 2.500 francs, 17,2 points below 3.000 and 24,1 points below 3.500. In the bracket of at least 5.000 francs, the gap is 18,9 points, this time in favor of men. These calculations were obtained by subtracting the values reported by the source: they do not indicate a change over time, because the thresholds belong to the same survey.
The sequence of thresholds makes the comparison clear without turning it into a forecast: as the threshold considered increases, the distance between the female and male shares grows in the lower brackets, while the highest bracket shows a greater male presence. The source thus documents a different wage distribution between women and men among cross-border workers in the Canton of Ticino, without attributing the result to a single profession or a single sector. ## Working hours do not fully explain the gap
Beyond salary brackets, the research also considers the employment percentage. Full-time employment accounts for 85,3% of men and 51,1% of women. Among female cross-border workers, 48,9% work at a reduced employment percentage. The most common arrangements are 80% (18,2%), 70% (8,3%) and 60% (6,6%).
The comparison between the two shares of full-time employment produces a difference of 34,2 percentage points: 85,3% minus 51,1%. The 48,9%, on the other hand, indicates the share of female cross-border workers in reduced employment and is not the corresponding male percentage. The source does not provide that figure, so the correct comparison remains the one between the explicitly reported shares.
### Comparison under equal conditions
According to the analysis, part-time work alone is not enough to explain the difference. To isolate the gap, the researchers considered age, educational attainment, employment percentage and professional role together. Even with these elements held equal, female workers report on average approximately 520 fewer gross francs per month than men; a statistically significant difference.
> The gap “does not appear to be entirely attributable” to the other characteristics considered.
This passage adds a verifiable connection to the comparison of hours: on the one hand, the distribution of working hours is very different, with a gap of 34,2 percentage points in full-time employment; on the other, after considering the variables indicated by the research, a reported average difference of approximately 520 gross francs per month remains. The text does not present that figure as a salary threshold, a rate or a forecast, but as the average result of the comparison between the responses.
The reference period remains that of the online questionnaire completed in May 2026. For this reason, the income brackets and the average difference should not be read as a time series. The research provides a comparative picture of the sample: it shows both the extent of part-time employment and the gap that the researchers observe even after considering age, education, employment percentage and role. This is a useful distinction because it avoids reducing the entire salary comparison to the sole number of hours worked. ## Pension provision, maternity and collective bargaining
The chapter on pensions examines knowledge of one’s pension fund, that is, the second pillar, referred to here as LPP. 74% of women say they know little or nothing about how it works; among men, the share is 66%. The research indicates that the issue affects part-time workers in particular.
### The pension fund threshold
For 2026, the threshold triggering mandatory enrollment in a pension fund is 22.680 francs per year with a single employer. However, people holding several small jobs may remain without coverage even with a higher combined income. The publication gives the example of 15mila francs earned from each of two companies: neither employer, considered separately, is required to insure the worker.
On this front, Ocst and its national organization Travail.Suisse are calling for salaries paid by different employers to be counted together for pension purposes. The request is linked to the situation described by the research, in which reduced working hours and holding several jobs can affect second-pillar coverage.
### Maternity and the professional gap
Maternity is also among the topics addressed by the publication. In Switzerland, leave is 14 weeks; for fathers, the two weeks have been provided since 2021. Travail.Suisse and Ocst support a popular initiative, currently in the signature-collection phase, providing 18 weeks for each parent, which cannot be transferred between them. The stated aim is to ensure that the birth of a child does not continue to weigh almost exclusively on mothers’ careers.
The research proposes collective bargaining as a tool to counter the pay gap between men and women. In the preface, Contessa recalls the “urgent need for gender equity, both in terms of pay and employment.”
The documented scope remains wages, working hours, pensions and maternity for cross-border workers who work in Canton Ticino. To explore pension provision further, consult LPP e rendita.
*Source: [varesenews.it](https://www.varesenews.it/2026/10/anche-tra-i-frontalieri-ce-una-disparita-di-stipendi-tra-uomini-e-donne/2718043/)*
